idiom_name: (T) -> Boolean / (T) -> List<String> function types; fun interface Validator<in T>
implementation_notes: Kotlin's function types are the carriers and composing them is ordinary code: contramap is a lambda over a projection, divide is { v -> a(v) && b(v) }, choose is an exhaustive when over a sealed hierarchy. Declaration-site variance expresses the pattern's name in the type system - fun interface Validator<in T> states that the validator consumes T, so a Validator<Animal> is usable where a Validator<Cat> is expected. java.util.function.Predicate is available for interop and brings and/or/negate, but a Kotlin lambda is not implicitly a Predicate: SAM conversion applies to Java interfaces (Predicate { ... }) and fun interface lets you declare your own SAM type. There is no stdlib combinator layer, so the classic structure reduces to a function type plus hand-written combinators - no framework needed.
pitfalls: Kotlin does not convert Kotlin lambdas to java.util.function.Predicate implicitly - wrap with Predicate { ... } or declare a fun interface; passing a bare lambda where Java interop expects a Predicate does not compile.

A (T) -> Boolean function type carries no variance for callers: if a rule set is public API, declare fun interface Validator<in T> so contravariance is guaranteed by the signature rather than by convention.
Concatenating List<String> per rule allocates on every validation; in hot paths accumulate into a MutableList (or a Sequence of failures) instead.
